revolutionary-battles-1775-1776.works: Red and blue diamonds stand out on the pale basemap and the legend is three short lines, so 'who won' reads well from one projected screen. Colony names are printed on the map, and the circled anchor for a Major Port City is easy to tell from a plain anchor, even at the back of the room.

findings.where: q2-all and q2-bunkerhill views; Revolutionary War Battles; Q2 'Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?', steps 1-2
findings.what: Nothing on the map shows a battle's year. To sort 21 battles into 1775 and 1776 I have to open every diamond one at a time, and around Boston and New York they sit in stacks (Bunker Hill opens as 1 of 3), so it's a lot of clicking and paging at the front. Pairs working from the paper sheet can't get the years at all.
findings.why: In a 15-minute slot on one projector, two dozen pop-ups eat most of the time, and the class watches me click instead of looking at the pattern the question is about.
findings.suggestion: Show the year on the map: label each diamond with its year, or add two bookmarks or filtered views ('Battles of 1775', 'Battles of 1776'), or give 1776 battles a different outline listed in the legend. Then one projected screen or a printed screenshot shows the shift from Boston to New York and New Jersey.

findings.where: q2-colony and q2-colony-ny views; Thirteen British Colonies; Q2 step 3 'Click the colony under each group of diamonds to read its name'
findings.what: Clicking inside Virginia and inside New York opens nothing. The colony names are printed on the map, so I can read most of them, but the red diamond furthest north on the St Lawrence has no name near it, and nothing on the map says that's Quebec.
findings.why: Students who follow the step will click, get nothing and decide the map is broken. The answer notes expect Quebec, and only that battle's pop-up can tell them.
findings.suggestion: Change the step to 'Read the colony's name on the map' (or turn on the colony pop-up), and add a 'Quebec (British province)' label.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-colony.png and --q2-colony-ny.png: '(no pop-up opened)'; --open.png and --q2-all.png show colony labels but none for Quebec

findings.where: q1-bookmark, q4-circles and q4-circle4 views; Turning Points drawn over Revolutionary War Battles; Q1 step 4 (Boston diamond) and Q4 steps 2-4 (Fort Washington, Fort Lee, Trenton)
findings.what: Once the numbered circles appear, circle 2 covers the Boston diamonds and circle 5 covers Trenton. I can't see a blue diamond at Trenton at all, though there is one in the zoomed-out view. Around circle 4 I can see two red diamonds but can't tell which is Fort Washington and which is Fort Lee, and clicking circle 4 opens a stack of 1 of 5.
findings.why: The sheet gives the diamond's colour as the only way to tell who won. If a circle covers it, the class can't see it on the projector, and I have to page through five pop-ups to find the fort we want.
findings.suggestion: Move the Turning Points circles to one side of their battles, or draw them smaller and hollow so the diamond shows through, and draw the battle diamonds above the circles.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q4-circles.png (circles 4 and 5; no blue diamond visible at Trenton, compare the blue New Jersey diamond in --open.png); --q4-circle4.png (pop-up '1 of 5'); --q1-bookmark.png (circle 2 at Boston, no diamond visible under it)

findings.where: q3-ports and q3-port views; Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781; Q3 steps 3-4
findings.what: The ports have no labels, so naming the major ports means guessing from the coastline and nearby diamonds. But clicking a small port did open a pop-up with its name ('Stonington, CT'), although the sheet and lesson page both say the layer has no pop-ups.
findings.why: From the front I can name the ports myself, but pairs on paper have nothing to go on. And students who read 'no pop-ups' won't try the click that actually answers the question.
findings.suggestion: Change the sheet to 'Click a port to read its name' (after checking that the five major ports have name pop-ups too), and label the five Major Port City symbols so a projected or printed view names them.

findings.where: q1-bookmark, q3-ports and q4-circles views; basemap; Q1 step 5 (Boston to Concord), Q3 step 5 (New York, Philadelphia, Boston), Q4 step 5 (New York City to Trenton)
findings.what: None of the places I'm told to measure between has a name on the map at these zooms: there are no labels for Boston, Concord, Philadelphia or Trenton. Even the Massachusetts label is missing from the Massachusetts bookmark view, because it sits up in present-day Maine.
findings.why: I have to point out the start and end of every measurement. Pairs will measure from the wrong diamond or anchor, and their answers will fall outside the accepted ranges.
findings.suggestion: Add a small labelled point layer for the places to measure (Boston, Concord, New York City, Philadelphia, Trenton), or label those diamonds and port symbols.

findings.where: q1-lexington and q2-bunkerhill views; Revolutionary War Battles pop-ups; Q1 step 2, Q2 step 2
findings.what: Below the date, the pop-up shows an empty white block where the picture should be, and the story only appears if I scroll past it.
findings.why: On our filtered network a picture from another site may never load. Projected, the empty block makes the pop-up look broken. The dates still show, so it's a nuisance, not a blocker.
findings.suggestion: Host the pictures in the same ArcGIS account as the map, or put the story text above the picture in the pop-up.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-lexington.png and --q2-bunkerhill.png (blank area under the date line)

roads-trails-and-rails-west.works: The opening view shows all seven trails from Missouri to the Pacific on one screen with a short legend, and each trail's pop-up has the trail's name as its title, so I can run Q1 from the front. The gray railroad pop-up is short and gives one clear year.

findings.where: open and q3-indigenous views; Trails West; Q1 step 1, Q2 step 1, Q3 step 3
findings.what: There are seven dotted lines in colours that are too close: Oregon and California are both olive, and Mormon Pioneer, Old Spanish and Pony Express are near-black, dark brown and dark red. Along the Platte, four trails run on top of each other. On the projector I can't match a line to the legend.
findings.why: Neither one projected screen nor a printout lets students match the legend to a line. They have to click, and pairs on paper can't follow a single trail from end to end.
findings.suggestion: Label each trail with its name along the line, repeated, and spread the colours further apart (for example Oregon green, California blue, Mormon Pioneer purple) while keeping the dotted style.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--open.png (legend swatches); --q3-indigenous.png (Oregon, California, Mormon Pioneer and Pony Express overlapping across Nebraska)

findings.where: q2-oregon view; Trails West; Q2 step 2 'Click the Oregon Trail and read its length and how many people traveled it'
findings.what: Clicking the Oregon Trail line opened the Pony Express Trail pop-up, marked 1 of 4. I have to page through the stack to reach the Oregon pop-up.
findings.why: Fine once I know, but students clicking on their own will copy the Pony Express figure (1,800 miles) as the Oregon Trail's length.
findings.suggestion: Say where to click: 'Click the Oregon Trail in Idaho or Oregon, where it runs on its own', or add an Oregon Trail bookmark centred on a stretch that carries only that trail.

findings.where: q4-railroads view; Railroads 1826 to 1911 and Transcontinental Railroads completed by 1911; Q4 steps 1-2
findings.what: Turning on Railroads turns on both layers. At the whole-country view, the 'thin gray' lines draw as a black mesh over everything east of the Rockies and much of the West, so most of the dotted trails disappear. The five thick lines show, but the trails they should be compared with don't. I also have to scroll the legend panel to reach Southern Pacific.
findings.why: Comparing rails with trails is the point of Q4, and on a projector the back of the room will see only a black mass.
findings.suggestion: Draw Railroads 1826 to 1911 in a lighter, semi-transparent gray, or leave it off inside the Railroads group so only the five thick lines come on first. Add an Omaha to Sacramento bookmark for the comparison.

findings.where: q3-indigenous view; Indigenous Territories; Q3 'Whose land?', steps 2-4
findings.what: The shading stops along a straight vertical line in Wyoming and a straight line along the Wyoming-Colorado border. Two quarters of the screen are blank, so the trails across central and western Wyoming, around Rock Springs, run over land with no territory on it.
findings.why: The sheet asks 'Was the land the trail crossed empty?' If the layer only partly draws, which is just what a slow school connection would show, the map seems to answer yes. I'd check whether this is the layer still loading or a real gap in the data.
findings.suggestion: Open this view on a slow connection. If it's a drawing problem, publish the layer so it draws whole (for example with simplified polygons). If the data has a gap, send students to a stretch that is covered, such as Nebraska.

findings.where: q3-indigenous view; Indigenous Territories labels; Q3 steps 2 and 4
findings.what: Only four names show across the whole view, in small gray type on coloured shading, and several are in the nations' own languages: 'Tsésthóe (Cheyenne)', 'Oóhenumpa', 'Sicangu', 'Pa'ka'to'de'uk'ethi' (Ponca)'. The see-through shapes overlap, so it's hard to say which territory the trail is actually crossing, and one name sits under the legend panel.
findings.why: From the back of the room the names are hard to read, and students won't recognise some of them as nations, so 'find two nations' turns into guessing.
findings.suggestion: Use larger labels with a white halo, placed more than once inside big territories. Add a line to Reading the map saying some names are in the nation's own language.

findings.where: open and q4-railroads views; basemap; Q2 step 4 'Use Measure for a straight line from Independence to Portland, Oregon'
findings.what: At the whole-country view Seattle and San Francisco are labelled but Portland isn't, and neither is Independence (Kansas City is). I can't tell from these pictures whether they appear when zoomed in.
findings.why: Pairs measuring on their own may stop at Seattle or at the trail's last dot. It's small, but it puts answers outside the range.
findings.suggestion: Add 'Independence' and 'Portland' labels at the Oregon Trail's two ends, or have the sheet say 'Portland is where the Oregon Trail ends, on the Columbia River'.

us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850.works: The opening view shows the whole country on one screen: the brown/green split, the Missouri Compromise line and the black slave-trade lines converging on the Gulf. Turning off the Underground Railroad routes makes the black lines stand out cleanly, and the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark has town names you can read along the orange routes.

findings.where: q1-pennsylvania and q2-missouri views; US States and Territories 1850; Q1 steps 2-3 (and the lesson page's 'match each shade to its legend group')
findings.what: When I click a state, it fills with a bright teal highlight. Pennsylvania, a free (brown) state, turns blue-green while its pop-up is open, which is the slave-state colour family.
findings.why: The class watching the projector sees a free state turn green just as I ask them to match its shade to the legend. I'd have to close the pop-up every time to show the real colour.
findings.suggestion: Set the selection highlight to an outline with no fill (or to a colour outside the brown/green scheme) for this map.

findings.where: open and q3-slavetrade views; US States and Territories 1850 legend; Q1 step 1 'find the four groups'
findings.what: The four groups are muted pinkish-brown and gray-green, and the two paler 'by compromise' shades sit close to the gray background. Each legend entry is a long quote from the source, and I have to scroll the panel to reach the slave-state groups.
findings.why: Projectors wash out pale colours. Brown against green will probably survive, but 'free' against 'free by compromise' may not at the back of the room, and with the legend scrolled the class never sees all four groups at once.
findings.suggestion: Use stronger fills, with hatching for the two 'by compromise' groups, and short legend labels ('Free state', 'Free by compromise', 'Slave state', 'Slave by compromise'), leaving the long source wording in the pop-up.

findings.where: open, q3-slavetrade and q2-line views; basemap and US States and Territories 1850; Q1 steps 2-3, Q3 steps 2-3
findings.what: At the whole-country view, no state is named, so every name has to come from a click. Zoomed in, faint gray modern names appear, including Oklahoma, Colorado and Wyoming, which didn't exist in 1850.
findings.why: Pairs on paper, or a class watching one screen, can't name the states the questions ask about unless I click every one. Modern names will turn up in answers about 1850.
findings.suggestion: Label US States and Territories 1850 with its own 1850 names at the opening scale (dark text with a halo), and use a basemap without modern state labels.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--open.png (no labels); --q2-line.png (faint modern labels such as OKLAHOMA, COLORADO, WYOMING)

findings.where: q2-line view; Missouri Compromise Line; Q2 step 2 'Click it and read its pop-up'
findings.what: Clicking the dashed line opened the 'Unorganized Territory' pop-up instead of the line's own pop-up, and there was no 1 of 2 to page to.
findings.why: The line is thin and hard to hit from the front with a trackpad. The territory pop-up does give 1820 and 'Free by Missouri Compromise', so students can still get the year, but not the note that Missouri was the exception.
findings.suggestion: Make the line easier to hit with a thicker symbol, or with a wider transparent line underneath that carries the same pop-up.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q2-line.png: pop-up 'Unorganized Territory ... in 1820 ... Free by Missouri Compromise'

findings.where: q4-bookmark view; Underground Railroad Approximate Routes and Cities; Q4 'Routes to freedom', steps 1-3
findings.what: The bookmark frames Illinois, Indiana and western Ohio. The routes run off the top and the right-hand edge, the black Canada dots are off screen or under the legend (only 'Cha...' shows by Detroit), and Toronto and Montreal are out of view.
findings.why: The question is 'Where do the routes lead?' The answer, Canada, isn't on the screen the bookmark gives, so I have to pan and zoom out while the class waits.
findings.suggestion: Widen the bookmark north-east to take in Lake Erie and southern Ontario, or add a second bookmark, 'Routes to Canada'.

findings.where: q1-pennsylvania view; US States and Territories 1850 pop-up; Q1 step 3 'read what year each became free or slave'
findings.what: The Pennsylvania pop-up says the state passed legislation against enslavement in 1780, then says the source records it as 'Abolition by state action between 1830-1850'.
findings.why: Students asked to read the year will see two dates and ask me which one is right.
findings.suggestion: I'd check the Harper's source category for Pennsylvania against the year field and fix whichever is wrong, or have the pop-up explain why they differ.

findings.where: q4-bookmark view; Cities labels; Q4 step 3 'read the names of the towns'
findings.what: The town names are orange text with no halo on the brown fill, and the basemap prints its own gray name beside some of them (Chicago, Detroit, Indianapolis, St. Louis).
findings.why: They read fine on a laptop. Projected, orange on brown is faint, and the doubled names look like two places.
findings.suggestion: Give the Cities labels a white halo, and turn off the basemap's place labels or use a basemap without them.

civil-war-battlefields.works: The opening view shows the 1863 states with their names in five clearly different shades, so which side a state was on, and the new state of West Virginia, can be read from one projected screen. At the Washington zoom, the District of Columbia label and the white dashed boundary make the border-state question easy to see.

findings.where: q3-railroads view (states layer off); Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static) and Boundary between Union and Confederacy; Q3 'Railroads, North and South', steps 1-3
findings.what: With the states layer off and the view spanning Virginia, the Carolinas and Tennessee, there are no railroad lines at all. Railroads only appear when I zoom right in to a small area, as in the Antietam and Gettysburg close-ups. With the states off, the white dashed boundary almost vanishes on the cream basemap, and the state names go too.
findings.why: Q3 asks students to compare railroads north and south of the boundary. At any view wide enough to compare, the map shows no railroads, so the map can't answer the question, from the front or anywhere else.
findings.suggestion: Remove or widen the visibility range on Railroads 1826 to 1863 so it draws at the whole-East view, and give the boundary a dark casing so it shows without the states layer. Alternatively, keep the states on with a lighter fill instead of turning them off.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q3-railroads.png (no railroad lines); --open.png and --q2-dc.png (none at wider views); --q4-diamond.png and --q4-gettysburg.png (thin dark lines only at close zoom)

findings.where: q2-dc, q4-diamond and q4-gettysburg views; Civil War Battlefield Boundary and Civil War Core Areas; Q4 steps 1-2 'Click the tan shaded areas of two battlefields'
findings.what: The sheet says the battlefields are tan, but they draw light gray or cream, and in Virginia, which is filled tan itself, they almost disappear. At the Washington-Virginia zoom they don't show at all; they only appear when I zoom further in.
findings.why: I'll be telling the class to click the 'tan' areas in a state that is tan all over. They're hard to point to from the front, and pairs will click the state and get nothing.
findings.suggestion: Give the battlefield boundaries a dark outline, change the sheet to 'light gray areas', and add a bookmark on the Washington-Richmond corridor at a scale where they draw.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q2-dc.png (no battlefield areas visible); --q4-diamond.png (pale areas on tan Virginia); --q4-gettysburg.png (light gray on navy)

findings.where: q4-gettysburg view; battlefield pop-up; Q4 step 2 (lesson page: 'read the battle's name, acres and state')
findings.what: Clicking Gettysburg opens 1 of 2. The first entry says 14,508 acres and gives no state. The answer notes give 73,551 acres and a state code.
findings.why: The name is there, and that's all the sheet asks for. But if I read out 'acres and state' at the front, as the lesson page says, the numbers won't match the notes.
findings.suggestion: Add the state to the pop-up, or change the lesson page step to 'read the name and acres; use the arrows if it says 1 of 2'.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q4-gettysburg.png pop-up: 'GETTYSBURG ... It spans 14,508 acres.' with '1 of 2'

findings.where: open and q2-dc views; Civil War Battlefields over U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863); Reading the map and Q4
findings.what: Union Victory diamonds are the same navy as the Union states, and Confederate Victory diamonds the same brown as the first states to secede. The Gettysburg diamond nearly merges into Pennsylvania, and in the Deep South the brown diamonds disappear into the brown states.
findings.why: On a projector the diamonds get lost, and students may read a diamond's colour as whose land it's on rather than who won.
findings.suggestion: Give the diamonds a white outline, and use result colours that the states layer doesn't use.

findings.where: open view; legend panel and state labels; Q1 steps 1-2
findings.what: At laptop size the legend panel covers the north-east, and the five state groups come at the bottom of a long legend, below the casualty sizes, so I have to scroll to reach them. One casualty size is labelled '< 0'. The names of the eastern states (Pennsylvania, Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey, New England) are hidden under the panel or the big diamonds.
findings.why: Matching the shades of 16 states from the front means closing the legend, zooming in and scrolling back. And '< 0 casualties' will get questions.
findings.suggestion: Put the states layer first in the legend, relabel '< 0' (for example 'under 1,000'), and add a 'The East in 1863' bookmark framed so the panel doesn't cover the eastern states.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--open.png (legend text 'Total casualties ... < 0'; states legend cut off at bottom)

findings.where: q2-dc view; state labels; Q2 'The border states', steps 1-2
findings.what: At the Washington zoom, Virginia, West Virginia, Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and the District of Columbia are labelled, but Maryland isn't.
findings.why: Students asked which two states border the capital can see only one of them named. Step 1 of the sheet names Maryland, so they'll manage, but the map should show it.
findings.suggestion: Raise the Maryland label's priority so it draws at this scale, or use a bookmark at the scale of q4-diamond, where it does show.

findings.where: q4-diamond view; Civil War Battlefields pop-up; Q4
findings.what: The Antietam pop-up shows a broken picture with an 'American Battlefield Trust' link in its place, and the dates are in light gray italic type.
findings.why: On our filtered network that link may be blocked. Projected, light gray italic dates are hard to read, and the dates are what students need.
findings.suggestion: Set the date in dark, non-italic type, and host the picture with the map or remove it.

the-battle-of-vicksburg.works: The opening view is a ready-made projector screen: the river, the labelled pins, the yellow Vicksburg pin and the railroad with track marks running east through Edwards to Jackson all show at once. With Civil War Battlefields on at that scale, the May 1863 diamonds line up between Bruinsburg Bend and Jackson.

findings.where: q1-bookmark view; Key Places in the Union March to Vicksburg and Railroads 1826 to 1911; Q1 steps 1-4 and Q2 step 1
findings.what: The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark zooms in much closer than the map's opening view. Milliken's Bend, Edwards and Jackson are off the screen, Bruinsburg Bend is a pin on the bottom edge with its label cut off, and the railroad east from Vicksburg runs under the legend panel.
findings.why: Step 1 takes the class away from the view they need. On one screen I'd have to zoom back out before Q1 or Q2 can be answered.
findings.suggestion: Reset the bookmark to the opening extent (Natchez to Jackson, Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend), or take the bookmark step out of the sheet.

findings.where: open and q3-championhill views; Key Places pins; Q2 step 2 'Check which side of the river each pin is on'
findings.what: At the view where all five pins show, Milliken's Bend and Bruinsburg Bend sit on or right beside the river, among old river loops and the dashed state line, and there's no 'Louisiana' or 'Mississippi' label near the river.
findings.why: Which side of the river each place is on is the heart of Q2, and from the projector it's a guess for two of the pins.
findings.suggestion: Add Louisiana and Mississippi labels on each side of the river (or a light state boundary with labels), and check that each pin sits clearly on its own bank.

findings.where: q4-porthudson view; basemap; Q4 'Splitting the Confederacy', steps 1-4
findings.what: Zoomed out to the Gulf, the only state name I can see is Alabama. Louisiana, Texas and Arkansas aren't labelled, Memphis is off the top of the screen, and the pop-up covers the middle of the river.
findings.why: Step 4 says to read the state names on the basemap, but at this view they aren't there, so the answer to 'which states lie west of the river' has to come from me.
findings.suggestion: Add a 'Memphis to the Gulf' bookmark and a layer of state names (the 1863 states layer from the Civil War Battlefields map would fit).

findings.where: q3-battles view; Civil War Battlefields legend; Q3 and Q4
findings.what: On this map a Confederate victory is a gray diamond and Inconclusive is yellow. In the Civil War Battlefields lesson, the layer with the same name shows Confederate victories in brown and Inconclusive in white. The yellow Inconclusive diamond is also the same colour as the Vicksburg pin.
findings.why: If I teach the two lessons in the same week, students will carry the colours over and misread who won.
findings.suggestion: Use the same symbols for Civil War Battlefields in both maps.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q3-battles.png legend compared with civil-war-battlefields--open.png legend

findings.where: q3-championhill and q4-porthudson views; Civil War Battlefields pop-ups; Q3 steps 2-3, Q4 step 3
findings.what: The pop-ups show a broken picture ('Battlefield Trust page', 'Tap on image to view page') that links to an outside site, and the dates are in light gray italic type.
findings.why: Our district filter may block the link. Projected, light gray italic dates are hard to read, and the dates are the whole point of Q3.
findings.suggestion: Set the dates in dark, non-italic type, and host the picture with the map or remove it.

findings.where: open view; Railroads 1826 to 1911 legend; Q1 step 3
findings.what: The legend lists five transcontinental railroads (Union Pacific, Great Northern and so on) that aren't anywhere near Mississippi. Every line on this map is 'others'.
findings.why: Students reading the legend will go looking for the Union Pacific near Vicksburg.
findings.suggestion: Show only the 'others' symbol in this map's legend, relabelled 'Railroad (built 1826-1911)'.

findings.where: open view; Key Places pin label; Q2 step 1
findings.what: The pin reads 'Miliken's Bend', but the sheet says 'Milliken's Bend'.
findings.why: Small, but students working in pairs notice when the sheet and the screen don't match, and they'll ask.
findings.suggestion: Correct the label to Milliken's Bend.
